title: Add Confidence Scores on Mini-Whiteboards
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton extends his long-standing interest in student confidence scores from paper-based quizzes to mini-whiteboards. Students write their working, their answer, and a 0-10 confidence rating in the corner of the board, giving the teacher an instant map of both what students think and how sure they are of it. He walks through a worked example — adding fractions — and shows how the combination of answer and confidence should change the order in which a teacher calls on students: starting with no response, then a high-confidence error to surface a misconception, then a low-confidence correct answer to build reassurance, and finishing with a high-confidence correct answer that can model strong explanation. He also flags the hypercorrection effect as part of the rationale, and suggests gamifying the scores with points won or lost to keep students honest about their confidence.
points: Barton pairs mini-whiteboards with 0-10 confidence scores so the teacher can see, in real time, not just whether students got an answer right but how sure they were of it.
He sequences questioning by combining answer and confidence: no response first, then a high-confidence error, then a low-confidence correct answer, then a high-confidence correct answer.
The rationale draws on the hypercorrection effect, where high-confidence errors are more likely to be corrected by feedback than low-confidence ones, making them worth surfacing publicly.
To keep students honest, he suggests gamifying scores — awarding points equal to the confidence rating for correct answers and deducting the same for incorrect ones.
quotes: I think asking students to assign confidence scores to their answers (before they know whether that answer is right or wrong) is a good idea for a number of reasons

It sets up the potential for students to benefit from the hypercorrection effect , where high-confident errors are more likely to be corrected in the future following feedback than low-confidence errors

We tell our students to do their working out on the back of their boards, write their answers nice and big in the centre of the front of their boards, and write their confidence scores (0 to 10, with 10 representing the highest level of confidence) in a box in the top-right-hand corner.

Board 2 - High-confidence error: We could call upon this student next to draw out a common misconception. It is also important that we return to this student at the end of the questioning process to ensure they can identify their mistake and articulate the correct process so they may benefit from the hypercorrection effect.

Board 3 - Low-confidence correct answer: Calling upon this student next may prove a magical moment as they realise that, despite their doubts, they are correct and are probably better at maths than they think.

You can encourage this by gamifying things: tell students that if they get a question correct, they get a number of points equivalent to their confidence score. But if they get the question wrong, they lose a number of points equivalent to their confidence score!
